messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Vignette:
Daniel was 56, a European American man who had spent most of his adult life as a working musician, moving between rehearsals, club dates, and studio sessions with a steadiness that had once felt like a second home. He was married and still lived with his wife, but in the years since the assault his world had narrowed in ways that had surprised him and then, over time, come to feel inevitable. The event itself had occurred after an evening performance, when he had been pulled into a situation that turned violently sexual and left him injured, humiliated, and unable to make sense of the sequence as anything like a story. When he tried to speak about it later, he found that he could not get the events into order. Some moments were startlingly sharp: a flash of blood, the harsh sensation of being overpowered, the smell of a particular cologne that seemed to hang in the air and return without warning even years later. Other parts were blank, inaccessible, as though his mind had shut doors before he could go through them. He described himself as pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, as if approaching it too directly would break something open he could not control.

In the weeks and months that followed, Daniel began organizing his life around places that felt safe enough, and those places were few. His home became the main one, along with a small handful of familiar spaces where he knew the layout, the exits, and the people. Outside of those limited settings, he felt exposed and on edge, especially in environments that reminded him of the loss of control he had experienced. He became wary of authority figures and anyone in uniform, including security staff, police officers, and even building personnel in venues where he used to work without hesitation. He said that when he saw someone in authority, something in him tightened immediately, as if he were bracing for another forceful intrusion. He also began avoiding people he had socialised with before the assault. Former colleagues, acquaintances from the music scene, and friends from that period had once been part of the ordinary rhythm of his life, but now even the idea of running into them could stir a heavy discomfort. He did not want to field questions, and he did not want to be seen in the changed state he felt he had become.

Daniel’s work as a musician remained part of his identity, but it too shifted. Certain venues and rehearsal spaces felt tolerable only if they were predictable and familiar, and he increasingly declined opportunities that would put him in crowded, less controllable settings. His wife noticed that he was shorter with people than he had used to be, and Daniel himself recognized that he had become irritable in ways that embarrassed him. He could snap suddenly, sometimes with an edge of aggression that he did not like in himself, and then retreat into silence. He made a deliberate effort to never allow himself to feel or express anger, partly because anger seemed dangerous to him and partly because he feared that if he let it surface, it would become unmanageable. Yet even as he kept it buried, he remained reactive to things that startled him. A sudden movement by another person could put him immediately on guard, his body tensing before he had even understood what had happened. He found himself scanning for the next abrupt gesture, the next possible violation of space.

The most vivid reminders could arrive from the ordinary life around him. Blood, even in minor settings, was enough to jolt him back into the sensory edge of the assault. A cut finger in the kitchen, a nosebleed on television, a smear on a bandage could leave him shaken and preoccupied. The smell of a specific perfume or cologne was equally potent. If he caught it in a hallway, at a restaurant, or drifting from someone in a crowd, he would feel his stomach drop before he could reason with himself. These moments were not dramatic in the eyes of others, but for Daniel they had the force of immediacy, as if the past had entered the room without warning.

By the time he came for help, his marriage had absorbed much of the strain of his narrowed world. He was still functioning, still working selectively, still showing up, but his life felt arranged around avoidance and vigilance. What finally brought him in was not a single collapse but the cumulative burden of feeling unsafe almost everywhere, of watching himself react with irritability and anger he refused to show, and of realizing that he could no longer tell a clear account of what had happened even to himself. He hoped therapy might help him understand why the memory remained so fragmented and why the world had become so restricted, though what frightened him most was the possibility that it would stay this way—that he would remain trapped in a life defined by only a few safe places and by a past he still could not fully face.
